analysis.one_liner: Repeals Clean Air Act limits on toxic air pollution from industrial facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one House member with no cosponsors, died in committee without ever getting a vote, and federal toxic air pollution standards stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-line bill would have deleted Section 112 of the Clean Air Act, the part of federal law that lists hazardous air pollutants, like known carcinogens, and sets emission limits on the factories and refineries that release them. Had it passed, industrial sources of toxic air pollution would no longer have faced those federal standards. It was introduced on October 6, 1994, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never moved again before the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.who_benefits: Industrial facilities that emit hazardous air pollutants, such as chemical plants, refineries, and other large factories, would gain by no longer facing federal emission standards for listed toxic pollutants, cutting their compliance costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Chemical plants, refineries, and heavy industry

how_it_helps.text: Repealing Section 112 would remove the federal requirement to list hazardous air pollutants and set emission standards for sources that emit them, eliminating compliance obligations for industrial emitters of toxic air pollution.

analysis.who_pays: People living near and downwind of industrial facilities would bear the cost, through increased exposure to hazardous air pollutants that federal law currently limits, including pollutants linked to cancer and other serious health harms.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the repeal argued that Section 112's technology-based standards impose significant compliance costs on industrial facilities, costs that can be passed on in higher prices and that can discourage domestic manufacturing.
The bill offered no replacement program: it simply deleted the hazardous air pollutant provisions, leaving no federal standards for toxic air emissions in their place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's only benefit was lower compliance costs for industrial polluters. The cost would have been the removal of federal limits on toxic air emissions, with no substitute protections, shifting health risks onto people living near and downwind of major industrial sources. On balance, the bill traded public health protections for industry cost savings, and it was so narrowly supported that it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom DeLay introduced the bill on October 6, 1994, to repeal Section 112 of the Clean Air Act, the hazardous air pollutant provisions.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and no further action was taken.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead: federal standards limiting toxic air pollution from industrial facilities remained in force because the repeal never advanced. No industry gained, since the bill's only purpose was removing those standards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities breathing the air near industrial plants

for.name: Rep. Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Clean Air Act's hazardous air pollutant provisions and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action on it, letting it die without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of any potential floor fight is unknown.

industries.note: These facilities are the major emitters of the hazardous air pollutants covered by Section 112. Repealing it would have eliminated their federal emission standards, with the savings coming at the expense of air quality for nearby and downwind communities.

industries.industry: Other large industrial sources of toxic air emissions (power plants, metals, and manufacturing facilities)
industries.note: Section 112 sets emission standards for industrial sources of listed hazardous air pollutants. Repeal would have freed these sources from federal toxic emission limits.
